title: Plotting earthquakes and volcanoes
body: A student studies a world map of earthquake epicentres and volcanoes. She notices a line of dots running through the central parts of the Atlantic Ocean, almost parallel to the coastlines on either side. The line extends into the Indian Ocean and splits a little south of the Indian subcontinent, with one branch moving into East Africa and the other meeting a similar line from Myanmar towards New Guinea. A second, broader shaded belt follows the Alpine-Himalayan mountains and the rim of the Pacific Ocean. Her teacher tells her that earthquakes in the two belts differ in the depth of their foci and asks her to relate the first line of dots to the relief of the ocean floor revealed by post-World War II mapping.

title: India's journey north
body: A geography class traces the position of the Indian subcontinent over time. About 140 million years ago the subcontinent lay as far south as 50 degrees S latitude, separated from the Eurasian plate by the Tethys Sea. As the Indian plate moved northwards, a huge outpouring of lava began around 60 million years ago and continued for a long period, building the Deccan Traps. From about 40 million years ago onwards, after the collision of India with Asia, the Himalayas began to rise, and scientists believe they are still rising today. The students are asked to locate India on a map for each of these events.
